729.title: Karna's abandonment
729.hook: a son is born shining, in armor and earrings, and his young mother sets him on the river
729.carry: a person on each side of it
729.howItsDone: Some retellings of the Mahabharata, in storytelling, dance and theater, linger on Kunti at the riverbank, letting audiences sit with her grief rather than rushing past it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Karna's abandonment began: Pritha, Durvasa's mantra, and the sun answering a girl's curiosity — "I only wanted to see if it worked." Did you pause before trying something just to see? Day seven hundred twenty-nine.

A baby is born in secret, and he's already dressed for battle. That's how the Mahabharata describes him: born wearing armor that's part of his own body, with bright earrings in his ears, shining like his father, the sun. Any other newborn would be scandal enough for an unmarried girl in a king's house. This one glows. There's no hiding him in a corner. And his mother is still very young, still living as a daughter under her father's roof. Today is the day the abandonment actually happens.
screen: `BORN IN SECRET.` → `ARMOR AND EARRINGS.` → `SHINING LIKE THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Kunti's choice is quick in the telling, and heavy in the hearing. Afraid of what her family and the world will say, she places her newborn son in a basket and sets it on the river. In one later part of the poem, the scene is told again at length: she weeps over the basket and speaks to the child, asking the gods of the waters, the sky and the earth to keep him safe, and saying that whoever finds him will be blessed to raise him. Then the current carries him away. Listen to the word the text chooses. It doesn't call her cruel. It calls her afraid. It tells us exactly why, and then it lets us watch her grief. Some readers hear a mother failing her child. Some hear a frightened girl doing the only thing she could see to do. Some hear both at once, and the poem seems to allow that. And notice the armor. The baby is sent off alone, but he isn't sent off unprotected. Whatever the river does, he's wrapped in his father's gift. Those earrings and that armor will matter enormously later, in a scene we'll come to. For now they're a quiet promise in the basket. The word abandonment can sound like a verdict. In this story, it's also an event with a person on each side of it. A mother on the bank. A child on the water. And the Mahabharata will spend a very long time following both of them.
screen: `SHE SETS HIM ON THE RIVER.` · `THE TEXT SAYS: AFRAID.` · `A FAILURE, A FEAR, OR BOTH?` · `WRAPPED IN HIS FATHER'S GIFT.` · then, large: `A PERSON ON EACH SIDE.`

segments.voice: This one is tender, so take your time. Let the breath move slowly. Let one decision come to mind that someone made about you before you could have a say: a move, a parting, a name. You don't need to forgive it or defend it. Just see that there was a person on the other side, deciding. Then notice what went with you anyway, the way the armor went with the child: something that kept you. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
Karna's abandonment. A son born shining in armor and earrings, set adrift by a frightened mother who blessed him as he went.
Your line: a person on each side of it. Today, when you hear about someone's hard choice, look for the fear behind it before you judge. Day seven hundred twenty-nine.

730.title: Karna's abandonment
730.hook: a charioteer and his wife find a basket on the river, and raise the boy inside as their own
730.carry: let go upstream, taken in downstream
730.howItsDone: In retellings, Karna is also called Radheya, son of Radha, honoring the mother who raised him; listeners meet him under that name as well as Karna.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Karna's abandonment happened: a shining baby in a basket, and a frightened mother blessing him from the bank — a person on each side of it. Did you look for the fear behind someone's hard choice? Day seven hundred thirty.

Downstream, a man and his wife are by the water. He's Adhiratha, a charioteer, a suta, someone whose work is driving and caring for the chariots of warriors. She's Radha. The text tells us they have no child. And floating toward them comes a basket. They pull it to the bank, open it, and find a baby boy, glowing, in armor and earrings. Yesterday we stood with the mother who let go. Today the story crosses the river and stands with the parents who catch.
screen: `DOWNSTREAM: ADHIRATHA AND RADHA.` → `A BASKET ON THE WATER.` → `A BOY INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Adhiratha and Radha take the boy home and raise him as their son. There's no hesitation in the telling, no long debate. They wanted a child, and here is one. They give him a name: Vasusena. The name points back at what he was found wearing, the armor and earrings he was born with. Later the world will know him as Karna. He's also called Radheya, son of Radha, after the woman who raised him, not the one who bore him. Hold onto that name. Now here's what the river has done. Karna was born to a princess and a god. He's grown up in the house of a charioteer. In the world of the Mahabharata, that matters. Birth decides a great deal: who may compete, who may rule, who gets laughed at. For most of his life Karna will carry royal blood he doesn't know about, and a charioteer's home he will not disown. Both will be pressed on him by others, and both will be part of who he is. And one more thing to notice. Abandonment is only half of this story. The other half is adoption. A child let go upstream is taken in downstream. Karna will carry both halves all his life: the loss from upstream, and the home from downstream.

Picture their face for a moment. Remember one specific kindness, the smallest one you can find: a meal, a lift, a word at the right moment. Let it sit in the chest, without needing words. The bell holds the time.

731.title: Karna's abandonment
731.hook: the boy grows up worshipping the sun, and one morning a stranger asks him for the armor he was born in
731.howItsDone: In Hindu storytelling Karna's name is tied to giving: his gift of the armor to Indra is retold as a picture of keeping one's word to give, whatever it costs.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Karna's abandonment, the other half: a charioteer and his wife catching the basket downstream — let go upstream, taken in downstream. Did you thank someone who took you in? Day seven hundred thirty-one.

Every morning the young man stands facing the sun, hands joined, praying. He stays there until the sun is high and its heat is on his back. That's Karna, grown. He doesn't know the sun is his father. And the text adds a detail about these hours of worship: while he prays, there's nothing he will refuse a Brahmin who asks for it. Today a stranger comes during that hour. And what he asks for is the one thing Karna was born wearing.
screen: `HE FACES THE SUN EACH MORNING.` → `WHILE HE PRAYS, HE REFUSES NO BRAHMIN.` → `A STRANGER COMES.`

segments.voice: The stranger is dressed as a Brahmin, a priest. But the Mahabharata lets us in on the secret: he's Indra, king of the gods, and the father of Arjuna, one of the five brothers. Indra knows that as long as Karna wears his armor and earrings, nobody can beat him. So he comes to ask for them as alms. The Adi Parva tells this scene early, beside Karna's birth, though in the story's order it comes years later. In a later book of the poem, the sun himself warns Karna in a dream that Indra is coming, and tells him to refuse. Karna answers that he can't. He's given his word to give, and he'd rather lose his life than his name for giving. So the Brahmin asks. And Karna takes a blade, cuts the armor from his own body, cuts the earrings from his ears, and hands them over. Indra, the text says, is pleased, and he gives Karna a weapon in return, a dart that can kill one enemy. Now set this inside our story. Karna was abandoned once already, set adrift by a mother who couldn't keep him. The armor was the one gift from his father that went with him. And today he gives it away with his own hands. The poem doesn't stop to call it wise or foolish. It shows the blade, and the gift. And it makes plain that the boy who lost so much at the start of his life chooses, here, to lose more, because someone asked.

segments.voice: Come to stillness, facing whatever light is near you: a window, a lamp, the sun if it's out. Let the breath settle. Ask yourself, quietly, what you find hard to give. Time. Attention. Forgiveness. Something you own. Don't force an answer, and don't promise anything yet. Just hold the question in the light for a while, and see what rises. The bell holds the time.
Karna's abandonment. The child set adrift grows into a man who gives away even his father's armor, cut from his own body, because someone asked.
Your line: he gives because someone asked. Today, when someone asks you for something small, notice your first answer before you give your real one. Day seven hundred thirty-one.

732.title: Karna's abandonment
732.hook: at the princes' tournament a stranger walks into the arena and matches Arjuna, and one woman in the stands knows him
732.howItsDone: The tournament scene, with Karna's entrance and Kunti's fainting, is retold by Mahabharata storytellers and on stage, where it lets the audience see what the characters can't.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Karna's abandonment, a stranger asked for the armor, and Karna cut it from his body — he gives because someone asked. When someone asked you for something, what was your first answer? Day seven hundred thirty-two.

Yesterday's scene came from further down the road; the poem tells it early, but it happens later. Today we step back into the order of events, and Karna still wears his armor. The scene is a great arena in Hastinapura. Drona, the teacher of the princes, has arranged a day for them to show the city what they've learned. The stands are packed. The royal family is there, Kunti among the women. The cousins ride and fight and shoot. And Arjuna outshines them all, the text says, with feats that leave the crowd roaring. Then a sound at the gate. Someone new walks in.
screen: `A DAY TO SHOW THEIR SKILL.` → `ARJUNA OUTSHINES THEM ALL.` → `A SOUND AT THE GATE.`

segments.voice: It's Karna, tall and shining, in his armor and earrings. He barely bows to the teachers. He turns to Arjuna and says, in effect: everything you've done, I'll do. And he does, one feat after another, while the crowd stares. Duryodhana is overjoyed. Here at last is someone to match the brother he resents, and he embraces Karna like a friend. Then Karna goes further and asks to fight Arjuna, one against one. And now the camera, so to speak, swings up into the stands. Kunti sees the armor and the earrings, and she knows. This is her son. The boy she set on the river is standing in the arena, about to fight another of her sons. The text says she faints. Vidura has her revived with cool water and sandal paste, and she comes to and watches, unable to say a word. Sit with how strange that is. Everyone else in the stands sees two rivals. One person sees two brothers. And she can't tell anyone. The abandonment wasn't only something that happened long ago by a river. It's still happening, in the silence of a mother in a crowd. Karna doesn't know. Arjuna doesn't know. Only Kunti, and us, the listeners, who've been let in on the secret. Every word spoken in that arena now means two things.

segments.voice: Let the body settle, and let the breath go quiet. Call up a crowd you were part of recently: a meeting, a game, a family gathering. Everyone in it was carrying something nobody else could see. Bring to mind one face from that crowd. Wonder, without guessing, what they might have been holding. Let that wondering soften how you see them. The bell holds the time.
Karna's abandonment. A stranger matches Arjuna in the arena, and in the stands, the mother who set him adrift knows him, and keeps silent.
Your line: she can't tell anyone. Today, in any crowd, remember that someone near you may be carrying a secret, and be gentle. Day seven hundred thirty-two.

733.title: Karna's abandonment
733.hook: asked who his father is, Karna has no royal answer; Duryodhana makes him a king, and an old charioteer walks into the arena
733.carry: it follows him into every room
733.howItsDone: In retellings, Karna's bow to Adhiratha in the arena is told as a sign of his loyalty to the father who raised him, and his friendship with Duryodhana is traced to this day.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Karna's abandonment, Karna matched Arjuna in the arena, and Kunti knew her son and kept silent — she can't tell anyone. Who in your crowd were you gentle with? Day seven hundred thirty-three.

Two fighters are ready to face each other. Then Kripa, one of the teachers, steps between them with a question that sounds polite. Arjuna is a prince, Kripa says, son of Pandu and Kunti. Tell us your mother and father, your royal line. A prince fights only an equal. And Karna, who has just matched every feat in the arena, has no answer to give. The text says he lowers his face. Here, on the last day of this part of the story, the abandonment comes due in public.
screen: `KRIPA ASKS FOR HIS LINEAGE.` → `A PRINCE FIGHTS ONLY AN EQUAL.` → `KARNA LOWERS HIS FACE.`

segments.voice: Duryodhana jumps in. If Arjuna will only fight a king, he says, then let Karna be a king. And there in the arena he has Karna crowned king of Anga. Karna, overwhelmed, asks what he can give in return. Duryodhana asks only for his friendship, and Karna gives it. Then, through the crowd, comes an old man, trembling, his cloth slipping. It's Adhiratha, the charioteer who pulled a basket from the river. And Karna, the new king, his hair still wet from the crowning, bows his head to him and greets him as his father. Adhiratha holds him and weeps. It's a beautiful moment, and it's the moment Bhima has been waiting for. You're a charioteer's son, he says, so pick up a whip. You're not fit to fight Arjuna, or to rule Anga. Duryodhana defends his friend: the origins of heroes, he says, like the sources of rivers, are hard to know. Look at the armor and earrings this man was born with. Then the sun sets, and the day ends with nothing settled. Look at the six days together. A girl's curiosity, a basket, a charioteer's home, an armor given away, a mother's silent recognition, and now a crown and an insult on the same afternoon. Karna's abandonment isn't one event. It follows him into every room. And the thing Kripa and Bhima hold against him, his birth, is the one thing he doesn't know the truth of.
screen: `DURYODHANA CROWNS HIM KING OF ANGA.` · `KARNA BOWS TO ADHIRATHA.` · `BHIMA: PICK UP A WHIP.` · `LIKE RIVERS, HARD TO TRACE.` · then, large: `IT FOLLOWS HIM INTO EVERY ROOM.`

segments.voice: Rest for two minutes with the breath. Bring to mind a time someone asked where you're from, or who your people are, and the question landed hard. Or a time you asked it of someone else. Just remember it. Then think of one thing you've done, not where you came from, that you're glad of. Let both sit side by side, the question and the deed. The bell holds the time.
Karna's abandonment. Asked his lineage, he lowers his face; crowned king, he bows to a charioteer; and the secret of his birth goes on following him.
Your line: it follows him into every room. Today, when you meet someone new, ask what they do or love before you ask where they're from. Day seven hundred thirty-three.

734.title: the lac house
734.hook: the city starts calling Yudhishthira its future king, and Duryodhana makes his father an offer: a holiday in Varanavata
734.howItsDone: The bait in this story is a festival of Pashupati, a name of Shiva; Hindus still worship Shiva as Pashupati, and the Pashupatinath temple in Kathmandu carries the name.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Karna's abandonment: a crown, a bow to the old charioteer, and an insult at sunset — it follows him into every room. Did you ask someone what they love before where they're from? Day seven hundred thirty-four.

Talk in the streets of Hastinapura: in squares and courtyards, people are saying Yudhishthira should be king. He's fair, they say, he's truthful, he's Pandu's eldest. Dhritarashtra is blind, so he was passed over before; why should his line rule now? Word of it reaches Duryodhana, and it burns. The Mahabharata gives him a long, anguished speech to his father. If Yudhishthira takes the throne, the crown will pass down his line, and we and our children will be shut out and disregarded. Today begins the lac house, and it begins with gossip.
screen: `THE STREETS TALK.` → `YUDHISHTHIRA SHOULD BE KING.` → `DURYODHANA BURNS.`

segments.voice: Duryodhana has a plan, and it's dressed up as a kindness. Send the Pandavas away, he tells his father, to the town of Varanavata, where a festival of Pashupati, a name of Shiva, is under way. Let them enjoy themselves for a while. Out of the capital, out of the people's eyes. Dhritarashtra hesitates. Pandu was good to me, he says, and the people love his sons; how can I do this? But he loves his own son, and in the end he agrees. So the old king calls his nephews in and speaks warmly about Varanavata: what a lovely town, what a festival, go and enjoy it. Yudhishthira sees the purpose behind it, the text says, but he's alone and without friends at court, and he agrees. Then Duryodhana calls a minister named Purochana, and gives him the real job. Go ahead to Varanavata. Build a fine house for the Pandavas. Build it out of lac and resin and other things that burn, and plaster it over so it looks like any house. Treat them well. Earn their trust. And one night, when they're asleep, set it on fire. Notice the shape of the plot. Nothing is done in the open. A father is persuaded. A holiday is offered. A house is built with care. Every step looks generous. That's the lac house before a single wall goes up: a trap made of kindness. And it can't happen without the blind king, who hesitated, and then said yes.

Don't scold yourself. Just look at the moment honestly, the way the story looks at Dhritarashtra. Where did you feel the hesitation? Notice that place now. The bell holds the time.
Purochana, the minister Duryodhana trusted to build a house of lac and resin in Varanavata, and to set it aflame.

735.title: the lac house
735.hook: as the Pandavas leave, Vidura warns Yudhishthira in words nobody else can follow, and in Varanavata the new house smells wrong
735.carry: this house is made to burn
735.howItsDone: Vidura is honored in Hindu tradition as a figure of wisdom and good counsel, and his coded warning at Varanavata is one of the scenes told to show it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lac house was planned: a holiday offered, a blind king persuaded, a house built to burn — a trap made of kindness. Did any offer make you ask what it was made of? Day seven hundred thirty-five.

A farewell at the edge of the city. The Pandavas and their mother are setting out for Varanavata, and a crowd has followed them out, unhappy to see them go. Vidura, their uncle, walks beside Yudhishthira. Then he says something strange. The words are in a tongue the crowd doesn't understand, the text says, a language that only Yudhishthira can follow. To anyone listening, it sounds like a riddle. To Yudhishthira, it's a warning. Today in the lac house, a message is passed in plain sight.
screen: `A FAREWELL AT THE CITY'S EDGE.` → `VIDURA SPEAKS IN A HIDDEN TONGUE.` → `A WARNING IN PLAIN SIGHT.`

segments.voice: Vidura's riddle goes something like this. There's a weapon not made of steel that can still destroy a body; whoever knows it can't be killed by it. A fire that burns a whole forest can't reach the creatures that live in holes underground. Someone who knows the roads, who can find the way by the stars, will survive. Fire, holes, roads, stars. Yudhishthira answers simply: I have understood. Later, on the road, Kunti asks him what all that was about, and he tells her: Vidura was warning us of fire. Then they arrive. Varanavata welcomes them with joy. Purochana greets them warmly, and after some days moves them into the new house. And Yudhishthira, walking through it, catches a smell: fat, and lac. He turns to Bhima. This house, he says, is made to burn. Now step back and look at this week. Karna gave away his armor. Karna walked into an arena and only his mother knew him. Karna was crowned and mocked in a single afternoon. And then a plot was laid, and a warning given in words no one else could read. It's a week of hidden things: a hidden brother, a hidden grief, a hidden trap, a hidden message. The Mahabharata keeps putting the listener in on secrets the characters don't share. Today, at least, one of the hidden things is caught in time.
screen: `FIRE, HOLES, ROADS, STARS.` · `I HAVE UNDERSTOOD.` · `THE HOUSE SMELLS OF LAC.` · `A WEEK OF HIDDEN THINGS.` · then, large: `THIS HOUSE IS MADE TO BURN.`

segments.voice: A week ends today, so take two slow minutes. Let the breath settle. Recall a warning someone gave you once, gently, maybe sideways, that you only understood later. Or one you were given this week. Who gave it? If thanks rises for them, even if you didn't listen, let it. Then just rest and notice the room you're in, its sounds, its smells, the way Yudhishthira noticed his. The bell holds the time.
Vidura, the uncle whose riddle of fire, holes, roads and stars warned Yudhishthira the new house was built to burn.
